According to data from the year 2022, the Devanagari Hindi script is spoken by over 342 million people worldwide and ranks third among the top 45 languages. There are approximately 11 vowels and 33 consonants and 10 numerals in the Devanagari script. The Devanagari script has no upper-or lower-case letters and is written from left to right. The data set includes 44 handwritten Devanagari vowels, consonants, and numbers (i.e., 4 Vowels, 30 Consonants, and 10 numerals) from 63 Devanagari character sets, 19 images from the character set were eliminated to avoid confusing humans and maintain usability. The final data set contains a total of 44,000 digitized images, 10,000 Devanagari numerals (10 numerals * 1000 each), 4000 vowels (4 vowels * 1000 each), and 30,000 consonants (30 Consonants * 1000 each), after the occluded images and scribbles have been removed. Each image has a grayscale data type and is in the .jpeg format. Each image requires 1.5 kb of storage and has a resolution of 65 by 65 pixels. Another class is for Devanagari Selected 10-numeral images. Each Numeral has one separate folder, so 10 folders are there in each folder 1000 greyscale images in JPEG format. The beauty of the dataset is that images from computer-literate users are gathered on a canvas made in Python. So there is no noise in any picture. fetched_contents.text: Handwritten Text Recognition for Low Resource Languages Abstract Despite considerable progress in handwritten text recognition, paragraph-level handwritten text recognition, especially in low-resource languages, such as Hindi, Urdu and similar scripts, remains a challenging problem. These languages, often lacking comprehensive linguistic resources, require special attention to develop robust systems for accurate optical character recognition (OCR). This paper introduces BharatOCR, a novel segmentation-free paragraph-level handwritten Hindi and Urdu text recognition. We propose a ViT-Transformer Decoder-LM architecture for handwritten text recognition, where a Vision Transformer (ViT) extracts visual features, a Transformer decoder generates text sequences, and a pre-trained language model (LM) refines the output to improve accuracy, fluency, and coherence. Our model utilizes a Data-efficient Image Transformer (DeiT) model proposed for masked image modeling in this research work. In addition, we adopt a RoBERTa architecture optimized for masked language modeling (MLM) to enhance the linguistic comprehension and generative capabilities of the proposed model. The transformer decoder generates text sequences from visual embeddings. This model is designed to iteratively process a paragraph image line by line, called implicit line segmentation. The proposed model was evaluated using our custom dataset (’Parimal Urdu’) and (’Parimal Hindi’), introduced in this research work, as well as two public datasets. The proposed model achieved benchmark results in the NUST-UHWR, PUCIT-OUHL, and Parimal-Urdu datasets, achieving character recognition rates of 96.24%, 92.05%, and 94.80%, respectively. The model also provided benchmark results using the Hindi dataset achieving a character recognition rate of 80.64%. Historically, handwritten text recognition, including Urdu and Hindi scripts, has been approached through segmentation at incremental levels of granularity—line, word, and character [11, 19, 25, 26]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks were commonly used in the initial wave of deep learning-based OCR models [31, 32]. Using region proposals for better feature extraction, Region-Based CNNs (RCNNs) [31] enhanced this architecture. However, as these models were trained character-by-character rather than word-by-word, they had a significant drawback: they ultimately required a separate language model. As a result, Transformer-based OCR (TrOCR) and other transformer-based OCR models were proposed in the literature [17]. In this approach, a pre-trained language model was employed for text production and substitutes a pre-trained Vision Transformer in the CNN layers. While improving over its predecessor, it has faced the inherent challenge of accurately defining and isolating individual entities (lines, words, and characters) for effective segmentation at each level. In contrast, we propose a new segmentation-free text recognition approach that directly recognizes text from paragraph images without explicit segmentation during the training and decoding phases. However, the leap to paragraph-level recognition introduces new complexities, such as varying text region/line numbers, diverse layout patterns and skews, and the imperative of defining a coherent reading order. A transformer-based decoder then generates an initial text output that undergoes contextual refinement. Finally, a pre-trained language model is considered to enhance coherence and fluency, ensuring high-fidelity text generation for document understanding and OCR-based tasks. Another source describes BharatOCR as a segmentation-free approach that avoids explicit line, word, and character segmentation and instead uses a pre-trained image encoder, a transformer decoder, and a pre-trained language model for refinement [N5-F4].

The evidence indicates that preprocessing and feature extraction are common early steps in the pipeline. One study describes the conventional ML pipeline as including classification, preprocessing, segmentation, and feature extraction for handwriting recognition [N1-R4]. Another study discusses feature computation aimed at extracting characteristics of handwritten strokes that depict the stroke’s class [N1-R3]. In the Devanagari-specific context, a holistic or segmentation-free approach is described, where the entire word image is treated as a single entity and features are extracted from the overall shape rather than from segmented components [N3-F3]. That study also reports the use of VGG16 as a feature extractor and evaluates the model using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, and AUC [N3-F3].

### Handling stroke segmentation and timing information

Stroke segmentation and timing information are central challenges in online handwriting recognition. The evidence shows that earlier OCR models were trained character-by-character rather than word-by-word, and often required a separate language model [N5-F4]. This suggests that segmentation was historically treated as part of the recognition pipeline rather than an ancillary task. ## 2. Major datasets and benchmark settings

- **Handwritten Devanagari Characters Dataset (IEEE Dataport)**: This dataset includes 44 handwritten Devanagari vowels, consonants, and numerals from 63 character sets, with 10,000 numerals, 4,000 vowels, and 30,000 consonants after preprocessing [N2-F2]. It also includes CSV files with training sets (70%) and testing sets (30%) [N2-F2].
- **Online digital handwritten Devanagari dataset**: A research paper describes the design of an online handwritten Devanagari dataset and uses it for recognition with deep learning [N2-R3].

- **Holistic Devanagari word recognition**: A study reports “exceptional accuracy,” with “impressive recall, high precision, and a remarkable F1-score” using VGG16 as the feature extractor [N3-F3]. It also reports AUC as an evaluation metric and notes that XGBoost achieved “the highest possible AUC” in the study [N3-F3].
- **BharatOCR segmentation-free Hindi/Urdu recognition**: The model reports benchmark results on Parimal Urdu (96.24%), Parimal Hindi (92.05%), and Hindi datasets (80.64%), and claims to outperform several state-of-the-art Urdu text recognition methods [N5-F4].

The evidence consistently frames some models as comparisons against baselines and state-of-the-art approaches. The holistic Devanagari study compares its proposed approach against existing state-of-the-art methodologies and reports strong performance across multiple metrics [N3-F3]. BharatOCR reports benchmark results on custom datasets and public datasets, and claims benchmark results on the NUST-UHWR, PUCIT-OUHL, and Parimal-Urdu datasets, with the Hindi dataset achieving a character recognition rate of 80.64% [N5-F4]. However, the evidence does not provide a single unified “state-of-the-art” benchmark across all Devanagari OCR studies; instead, results vary by dataset and task level (character, word, or paragraph-level recognition) [N1-R2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

### Common reporting gaps

The evidence highlights several common reporting gaps that affect reproducibility:

- **Test set leakage**: Random train-test splits can lead to data leakage, and traditional k-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation are default procedures that should be used carefully [N6-R2].
- **Confidence intervals**: The provided evidence does not uniformly include confidence intervals, so this is a recurring limitation in the reported results [N4-R3][N6-R2].

Feature extraction is often based on learned encoders such as VGG16, and preprocessing includes grayscale conversion, scaling, and fixed-resolution normalization [N3-F3][N2-F2].
